title: Leaders Without Character and Strong Values Have No Enemies and Make Poor Decisions
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Using Groucho Marx's quip about negotiable principles as a hook, this Field Note argues that leaders with weak or shifting values struggle specifically at the moment decisions must be made. Because every real decision creates winners and losers, a leader without a firm value system defaults to whatever choice upsets the fewest people rather than whatever choice is actually right. The piece frames this as a form of avoidance dressed up as diplomacy, and argues that grounding in stable, tested values is what allows leaders to accept the inevitable backlash that comes with real decisions.
points: Leaders with fluid or absent values tend to choose whatever option upsets the fewest people, not the best option.
Because decisions create winners and losers, weak character makes decisive action especially difficult.
Social media pressure and the volume of dissent are cited as forces that push leaders away from their values.
Strong, tested values are framed as what allows leaders to tolerate the backlash from difficult decisions.
The piece concludes that accepting you will upset people and make enemies is a requirement of leadership.
quotes: These are my principles, and if you don’t like them…well, I have others.” Some leaders don’t know their values.
This weakness in character is attractive to some leaders because it doesn’t ruffle feathers or make others uncomfortable.
The best leaders accept that making hard decisions will result in consequences that will upset at least some people.
True character lights the path to strong decisions. Accept that you’re going to upset some people and make some enemies. Leadership requires it.
